This word, among others, raises a huge problem in terms of the history of LJLA manuscript and language traditions. So what is to account for the appearance of this form?

notes.text: Levy connects the Nahum passage with the root rwy and argues that the word literally renders Biblical ṭyṭ, thus "mortar" or the like. But the passage is clearly rendered metaphorically in the Targum, and such an interpretation ignores the parallel usage in the Isaiah passage. Note that it is always used with שעבד, i.e. control your slaves more as they work in the mud. The unique Mandaic example may well be deemed a separate word, but we find no other form in the other dialects with which to connect it.

notes.text: Generally quite limited to specific usages (i.e. w. negative or kl) in the earlier dialects. The CPA form is probably a syriacism. At Palmyra both mdʕm and mdʕn are used, generally without distinction. In the Palmyrene Trf, however, the former form seems to mean "something" whereas the latter is something like "anything". In JBA, מידי predominates in the main Talmudic tractates while מידעם is regularly used in the "special" tractates and in the geonic literature, as pointed out by Epstein "Post-Talmudic-Aramaic Lexicography" pp.322f.

notes.text: The G stem appears in the passive participle almost exclusively, i.e., mṣy adj. Non-participial examples of G in Syriac (see LS2) should be considered dubious, for there is no clear example in our entire database, and only a very few clearly perfect forms in late texts from the other Eastern dialects. This is probably due to the fact that, at least in Mandaic, in earlier texts the adjectival form was also used in perfective contexts, as noted clearly in MD. It remains questionable whether a form such as mSun should be considered a finite verb rather than a 'finitized' adjective. In any case, there are no clear examples in any dialect of a prefixed G stem. The primacy of the participial form demonstrates that this is almost certainly a development from Akkadian maṣû with the same meaning and patterning.

formsNote: Originally absolute and construct māreʕ ( > mārē), emphatic māryā, but already in OfA the construct can appear simply as mār_. Regularly shortened as a title of respect to mār (i.e., from the first person suffixed form?) and regularly spelled ܡܪܝ in Syriac but simply מר in Jewish texts; pl. mārwān, mārayyā, and mārē, the latter especially in compounds. The full determined form is māryā, but in Syriac that is used only for the Lord God (ie. the Tetragrammaton) and a new form mārā based on the short abs. is used in other contexts, even regularly so in reference to Jesus. Note that in JLAtg the sg. and pl. constructs are both מָרֵי; in LJLA also מרוות

notes.text: NB: The semantic development is historically clearly from "province" to the large "capital" city of an administrative unit which can also be referred to by the same name/term, just as city-states in Antiquity were often called by the name of their capital city. In Christian times such a city would headquarter a bishop. A qryh is one of a number of large towns or villages within such a unit. A krk is somewhere in between, generally presupposing a surrounding wall. See, e.g., Jacob of Serough MemDan(Bedjan vol.2 #36) 102:17.

NB: Syriac only uses the aphel in the sense of "to reign". We have here assumed that in most cases in Syriac, the Gt is used for a single person taking advice from (b, ʕm) others, while the Dt is used when the subject is the entire group; however, the modern vocalizers of the NT seem to prefer to use the DT in all instances.

notes.text: Both the targum and the LXX understand this MT passage [כִּנְטוֹת יָדוֹ] to mean "when he raised/stretched his hand," properly so by the context of the previous verse, but it is by no means clear from the Syriac rendering that that is what is understood here. Our justification for this interpretation is that unlike the MT, the Syriac does not use the same verb for the action in verse 18.
